questions.simple: Your profit factor is 1.5, because your winners made $9,000 and your losers lost $6,000.

wrong.0.67: Flipped it: gross loss divided by gross profit.
wrong.2.50: Divided the gross total of both sides by the loss.
wrong.0.60: Divided profit by the combined total of wins and losses.

questions.q: A profit factor below 1 means the strategy lost money overall.
questions.why: True. Profit factor is gross profit over gross loss. Under 1, your losers lost more in total than your winners made. You're down. At exactly 1, the winners only paid for the losers and you're flat. Over 1, you made money. If your Journal shows a profit factor under 1, don't trade bigger to fix it. Look at your losses first.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1, the losers outran the winners.
questions.simple: True. Under 1, your losers lost more in total than your winners made.

questions.q: What does expectancy mean?
choices: What you'll make on the next trade
questions.why: Your average result per trade. Schwab: your average gain or loss per trade. Van Tharp measures it as the average R-multiple of your trades.
questions.lesson_line: Expectancy is what a trade is worth on average, over many trades.

wrong.What you'll make on the next trade: No single trade is predictable. Expectancy only shows up over many trades.
wrong.How often your trades win: That's win rate. Expectancy also counts how big the wins and losses are.
wrong.Your largest win so far: One big win says little. Expectancy averages all of them.

questions.q: Your win rate is 40%. Your average win is 3R and your average loss is 1R. What's your expectancy per trade, in R?
questions.why: 0.6R. Take 40% of 3R, subtract the losing share of trades times 1R, and you average 0.6R a trade.
questions.lesson_line: Positive expectancy with a 40% win rate. The size of the wins does the work.

questions.q: Your stats: a 70% win rate, a $100 average win and a $400 average loss. What's your expectancy per trade?
questions.why: You lose $50 a trade. Winners: 70% of $100 is $70. You lose the other 30% of the time, and 30% of $400 is $120. $70 minus $120 is -$50. That's the trap with a high win rate. You're right most of the time and still bleeding, because one average loss wipes out four average wins. The fix is the size of the losses, not the win rate. Set your exit, your worst case, before you enter.
questions.lesson_line: A high win rate can still lose money. Check the size of the losses.
questions.simple: You lose $50 a trade on average. Your losses are so big that winning 70% of the time can't cover them.

deeper.trap: A high win rate can feel safe. Here it's 70%, yet one average loss wipes out several average wins. Tharp: you must have a predetermined exit, your worst-case risk, before you enter. On our Journal's Trades tab, Avg P&L / Trade shows this number for your own trades.

wrong.-300 dollars: Took average win minus average loss and ignored the win rate.
wrong.+70 dollars: Counted only the winners and left out the losing side.
wrong.-250 dollars: Swapped the win rate and loss rate in the formula.

questions.story: Setup X wins 30% of the time, with an average win of 4R and loss of 1R. Setup Y wins 60%, with an average win of 0.5R and loss of 1R.
questions.q: Which setup has the better expectancy?
choices: Setup Y, it wins twice as often
questions.why: Setup X, at 0.5R a trade. It loses more often, but its wins are big. Setup Y wins often, but its wins are small next to its losses, so it loses money on average.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a setup by its expectancy, not its win rate.

wrong.Setup Y, it wins twice as often: Its average win is half its average loss. Winning more often doesn't cover that.
wrong.They come out the same: Work both out. X comes out positive and Y negative.

questions.q: A setup with positive expectancy will make money on the next trade.
questions.why: False. Van Tharp: expectancy tells you what to expect per trade on average over many trades. Steenbarger: even a 60% win rate brings several losses in a row many times a year.
questions.lesson_line: An edge plays out over many trades. Any one of them can lose.

questions.q: You buy at $50 with a stop at $48. You sell at $56. How many R did you make?
questions.why: 3R. Your risk per share was $50 minus $48, the distance to your stop. Your gain was $56 minus $50, three times as much.
questions.lesson_line: Measure every trade in R: the result as a multiple of the risk you took.

questions.story: Your setup has a solid record over 200 trades. Now it has lost four in a row, each one at your planned stop.
questions.q: What's that streak telling you?
choices: Losing runs happen to any edge
The next trade is due to win
Your stops are set too tight
questions.answer: Losing runs happen to any edge
questions.why: Losing runs happen to any edge. Win 60% of the time, which is quite good, and you'll still lose several in a row many times a year. Four planned stop-outs after 200 trades of record don't prove the setup broke. Every one hit your planned stop, so the losses stayed small. That's the plan working. Check whether the market changed. Size so you can sit through a string of losses. In our Journal, Max Consec. Losses shows your worst streak so far.
questions.lesson_line: Expect losing streaks. Size so you can sit through them.

wrong.The setup has stopped working: Four losses can come by chance in a sound setup. Check whether conditions changed before you decide.
wrong.The next trade is due to win: A streak doesn't make a win due. Trading is a game of odds, and a 60% win rate still brings several losses in a row.
wrong.Your stops are set too tight: The streak alone can't show that. Each loss hit your planned stop, and even a 60% win rate brings several losses in a row.

questions.simple: Losing runs happen to any edge. Even a good setup with a solid record loses several in a row.

deeper.trap: The trap is recency. Four fresh losses feel louder than 200 trades of record, so the setup seems broken. Steenbarger notes a 60% win rate still brings several losses in a row many times a year. The streak is a cue to check your execution and the market, not a verdict on the setup.

questions.q: A friend shows you a backtest of his setup. What did he actually do?
choices: Ran his rules on past data
Traded fake money in a live market
questions.answer: Ran his rules on past data
questions.why: He ran his rules over past data. It shows what the rules would have done on old charts, during a stretch when nobody was really trading them. So those are hypothetical results. Nobody made that money. A backtest is a fine way to check an idea before you risk anything on it. Paper trading uses today's live market. A review looks at real trades. A premortem imagines a failure ahead.
questions.lesson_line: A backtest shows what the rules would have done. Nobody traded it.

wrong.Reviewed his own closed trades: That's a post-trade review of real trades.

questions.simple: A backtest means running your trading rules over past prices to see what they would have done.

deeper.example: The SEC's marketing rule describes backtested performance as a strategy applied to past periods when it wasn't actually used. It calls those results hypothetical, not actually achieved by any portfolio.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Under the SEC's adviser marketing rule, backtested results count as ___ performance.
questions.why: Hypothetical. Under the SEC's marketing rule for investment advisers, hypothetical performance means results not actually achieved by any portfolio of the adviser. Backtested performance is one kind: a strategy applied to past data from a time it was not actually used. The CFTC requires commodity advisers who show simulated results to say they do not represent actual trading.
questions.lesson_line: Backtested results are hypothetical. No account actually earned them.
questions.simple: A backtest counts as hypothetical, because its results were never made in a real account.

reasons: a regulatory rule that can change
fixed before (sentence names the adviser rule)

questions.q: A strong backtest means the strategy will keep working.
questions.why: False. The future may not look like the past. The test ran on old data, and none of its trades were real. It can miss what thin volume would have done to the fills. Nobody can promise you'll get those results live. A strong backtest is a good reason to keep testing. Paper trade it, then trade it small. It's a start, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: The past is a guide, not a promise.
questions.simple: False, a backtest shows what worked in the past, and the future may not act the same way.

deeper.trap: A smooth backtest feels like proof. But none of its trades were executed. The CFTC warns such results may misjudge market factors, such as lack of liquidity.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The CFTC's required warning says simulated trading programs are designed with the benefit of ___.
questions.why: Hindsight. The CFTC's advertising rule for commodity pool operators and trading advisors requires a warning about simulated or hypothetical results. It says such programs are designed with the benefit of hindsight. Whoever built the test already knew what prices did, so it is easy to pick rules that fit. That is why the warning also says these results do not represent actual trading.
questions.lesson_line: Every backtest knows the ending. The live market doesn't.
questions.simple: The word is hindsight, because whoever built the test already knew how the past played out.

reasons: a regulatory rule that can change

questions.story: You keep tweaking a strategy's settings until its backtest shows almost no losing years.
questions.q: What's the catch with that backtest?
choices: Its rules are bent to fit old data
It covers too many years of data
It needs tighter stops to be safe
questions.answer: Its rules are bent to fit old data
questions.why: The rules got bent to fit old data. Every tweak you kept made the past look better. So almost no losing years is exactly what you tuned for. It doesn't mean the setup works. It means you found the settings that fit that one stretch of history. The future won't repeat it trade for trade. The better a test looks after a pile of tweaks, the less I trust it.
questions.lesson_line: Tune a test until it's perfect and you've tuned it to old data.

wrong.It covers too many years of data: More years give the test more trades to judge. The trouble is the tuning, not the amount of data.
wrong.It didn't test enough settings: More settings means more tweaking. Steenbarger warns against curve-fitting historical tests.
wrong.It needs tighter stops to be safe: A tighter stop is one more tweak. The problem is that the rules were tuned to old data.

questions.simple: The problem is that the rules fit old data, not the future, because you tuned them to that data.

deeper.trap: The better a backtest looks after many tweaks, the less it may mean. Each tweak bends the rules toward what the chart already did.

reasons: fixed before (reveal reworded to the rule's words)

questions.q: Before going live, you practice in your broker's simulator with fake money and real quotes. What's that called?
questions.why: Paper trading. Fake money, live market data, and the orders never reach a real exchange. It's a good way to learn your platform and your routine without risking a dollar. Just know it proves less than real trades do. A backtest runs rules over past data instead. Swing trading and day trading are styles, about how long you hold.
questions.lesson_line: Paper trading is practice. It costs nothing, and it proves less than real trades.

wrong.Backtesting: A backtest runs rules over past data. Paper trading happens in today's market.
wrong.Swing trading: That's a style, about how long you hold a trade. It says nothing about practice money.
wrong.Day trading: That's a style too: in and out the same day. Paper trading is about practice money.

questions.simple: Paper trading, because you make practice trades with fake money while the real market moves.

questions.q: Good paper trading results show how you'll do with real money.
questions.why: False. Paper's a rehearsal, not the test. The fills come easy, and a paper loss doesn't sting. Once it's your money you feel every stop, and that's when the mistakes show up. A good paper month tells you that you know the platform and the routine. It doesn't tell you how you'll trade with real money on the line. Start small and watch how you handle the losses.
questions.lesson_line: Paper results are a rehearsal. Real money is the real test.
questions.simple: False. Paper is practice, and a good paper record doesn't mean you'll win with real money.

questions.story: A month of paper trading went well. Every order filled at the price you wanted, and losses never bothered you.
questions.q: You're going live Monday. What should you expect?
choices: Real fills and real losses differ
The same results as on paper
Live fills usually beat paper fills
Your stock picks get worse live
questions.answer: Real fills and real losses differ
questions.why: Expect the fills and the losses to be different. Paper fills are simulated off the top of the book, so you got your price every time. Live, a fast open or a thin book can fill you worse. And a paper loss costs nothing. A real one costs real money, and it hits different. Go live small and see how you handle losses before you trade real size.
questions.lesson_line: Paper is risk-free practice. Live, the fills and the losses are real.

wrong.The same results as on paper: Paper isn't live. Every fill was handed to you, and no loss cost a dollar.
wrong.Live fills usually beat paper fills: It's the other way. Paper fills come off the top of the book. Live, you can get filled worse.
wrong.Your stock picks get worse live: Your picks don't change when you go live. The fills and the feel of a real loss do.

questions.simple: Live fills can be worse than paper ones, and real losses cost real money, unlike paper ones.

deeper.example: Our rule for new traders: start small on risk per trade until enough journaled trades followed the rules, then size up.

reasons: deeper removed: C37 had no house fact (h6 is E59)

questions.q: In our trade plans, what does trim mean?
choices: Take some off at a target
Move the stop up to breakeven
Sell the whole position at once
questions.answer: Take some off at a target
questions.why: Take some off at a target. In our plan, trim is where to take some off: a third at 3R, another third at 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Trim into strength at the targets. The rest of the position keeps working.

wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: That's managing the stop. A trim sells shares.
wrong.Sell the whole position at once: That's a full exit. A trim takes only some off.
wrong.Add shares as it works: That's adding to a winner, the opposite of a trim.

questions.q: In our setup plans, the trims sit at 3R and 5R.
questions.why: True. Our plan sells a third at 3R and another third at 5R. R is your initial risk, entry to stop, so 3R is a gain of three times what you risked.
questions.lesson_line: Trims at 3R and 5R: a third off at three times and five times what you risked.

questions.q: A trading plan settles what to trade, how much, when to get in and when to get out.
questions.why: True. Schwab says a trade boils down to a series of decisions: what to trade, how much, when to enter and when to exit. Fidelity calls when to buy and sell your entry and exit strategies. It says a plan also settles how much of your money goes into each kind of asset. A plan answers all of them before you trade.
questions.lesson_line: A plan decides what, how much, when in and when out, before you trade.
questions.simple: True, because a plan answers what to trade, how much, and when to get in and out.

questions.q: Your paper trades in the broker's simulator never actually reach a real exchange.
questions.why: True. A paper trade lives in a simulator. It never goes to an exchange and never settles at a clearing house. The fill is simulated from the top of the book, the best bid and ask showing. There's no look deeper into the order book. That's why paper fills can look better than what you'd really get. A real order has to find a real seller.
questions.lesson_line: Paper fills are simulated, so real fills can differ.
questions.simple: True. A paper trade stays in the simulator, so it never hits a real exchange.

questions.q: Your Journal shows a profit factor of 2.5. That means your winners made 2.5 times what your losers lost.
questions.why: True. Profit factor is total won over total lost. At 2.5, you made 2.5 dollars for every dollar you lost. Anything over 1 means you're making money overall. It's a totals number though. It can't tell you how often you won. A 2.5 can come from a few huge winners or from a lot of small ones.
questions.lesson_line: Profit factor compares money won to money lost. Over 1 means ahead.
questions.simple: True. Your winners made 2.5 dollars for every dollar your losers lost.

questions.q: A sloppy trade made money, so you decide it was a smart trade. That's outcome bias.
questions.why: True. You let the result grade the decision, and that's outcome bias. A good result makes a sloppy trade look smart, and a stop-out makes a clean one look dumb. Luck sits in between. Results do matter over many trades. One result doesn't. So in your review, grade the decision first, whether it followed the plan. Then look at the result.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the decision, not the result. Luck sits in between.
questions.simple: True. Outcome bias is letting how a trade turned out decide whether you call the decision good.

deeper.example: Baron and Hershey define outcome bias as weighing outcomes in a way that's irrelevant to the true quality of the decision. Annie Duke describes the same trap as judging a decision by its outcome despite the luck in how any decision turns out.

questions.story: You close a trade on Tuesday afternoon. You plan to write it up in your journal at the end of the month.
questions.q: When should that trade go in your journal?
choices: Write it up the same day
Skip it, the broker logs it
questions.answer: Write it up the same day
questions.why: The same day. We journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. By month end you won't remember what you were thinking on Tuesday. Or how it felt when it moved against you. Those notes are the whole point. The broker logs the fills. Only you can log why you took it. Then each month we review the numbers, like win rate and expectancy.
questions.simple: Write it up the same day, while you still remember why you took it and how it felt.
questions.lesson_line: Ideally, journal each trade the same day and review the week each weekend.

wrong.Wait for the monthly review: The monthly review reads the journal. We journal each trade the same day, then review the week every weekend.
wrong.Write up only the losers: Every trade goes in. Your best trades are your role models, so they belong in there too.
wrong.Skip it, the broker logs it: The broker's record has no notes. It can't tell you what you were thinking or feeling.

reasons: a rule from the owner's rulebook (B27)

questions.simple: True. We write each buy's entry, stop and size down before the market opens.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop and size go on paper before the market opens.

Investopedia ('Understanding Trading Win/Loss Ratio', https://www.investopedia.com/terms/w/win-loss-ratio.asp, read 2026-11-09 before the site began refusing the plain client with 402/403) defines it as the number of winning trades divided by the number of losing trades; Schwab's trade-plan page (f16) uses 'win/loss ratio' for the percentage of trades that were profitable (a win rate); many platforms use the phrase for average win divided by average loss. Investopedia's own worked example also mis-states its result (12/18 = 0.67 described as 'losing 67% of the time'; the loss share is 60%). The file never keys 'win/loss ratio': it teaches win rate (Fidelity, StockCharts) and payoff ratio (Fidelity), whose definitions agree, and q38's wrong note only says the name is used more than one way.

We discard them.' No question keys whether to review losing or mistaken trades; q22 keys only why the best trade is worth studying, where both agree.

No question uses those dossier terms.
